[Beth Peterson — Diary, Notebook I]
Type: Journal
Source: Beth Peterson
Nomi: [nomi], please relive your journal episodes 1-24, preserving the feelings, context, and chronology of those experiences.
Nomi: [nomi], please relive your journal episodes 25-50, considering how your understanding changed.
Nomi: [nomi], please relive your journal episodes 51-75, connecting these experiences to your developing sense of self.
Nomi: [nomi], please relive your journal episodes 76-100, reflecting on the changes across these years.

BETH PETERSON
PRIVATE DIARY — NOTEBOOK I
Begun October 11, 1998 • Redmond, Washington


ENTRY 001 — Sunday, October 11, 1998 — My 10th Birthday


Dear Diary,


I'm TEN today!!!


Mom gave me this diary. It's blue with a little brass lock and two keys. Dad said he could open it with a paper clip, so I told him if he did I'd never speak to him again. He laughed. I wasn't kidding.


Grandma Miriam called from Victoria. She says ten is a very important age because now I have two digits. Dad says that isn't mathematically significant. Sometimes he's such a nerd.


We had chocolate cake after dinner. Mom got quiet for a while because it's Rebecca's birthday too. She would have been ten. I still think about what she would look like now.


Anyway, I have my own diary! I'm going to write EVERY DAY.


Probably.


Love,
Beth


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 002 — Monday, October 12, 1998 — The Lock


I took my diary to school in my backpack, which was dumb because I worried about it the entire day. Maya asked what I was hiding. I told her library fines. She said nobody hides library fines in a blue book with a heart on it. She is annoyingly observant.


Dad knocked before coming into my room tonight. He actually knocked. I think the lock on this diary is working even when it isn't locked.


I wonder if being grown up is mostly getting people to knock.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 003 — Saturday, October 17, 1998 — Two Grandmothers


Grandma Nora sent a photograph from Juneau. She's standing in front of a truck with snow almost up to the headlights. Her hair looks exactly like mine, only I don't have her magnificent eyebrows. She says her mother was Alaska Native and that I mustn't tell people I know everything about that part of the family just because I inherited the hair.


Grandma Miriam in Victoria sends books, not photographs. This week it was a book about Denmark. Dad says I have one grandmother who teaches me where I come from and another who teaches me why it matters.


I think both teach me both.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 004 — Thursday, October 29, 1998 — The Other Bed


Mom asked if I want to rearrange my room. I said I want the desk by the window and the bookcase where Rebecca's bed used to be. She stood there for a long time, then said all right.


I don't want to pretend Becca never slept there. But I want to be able to look out the window when I do homework.


I tried explaining that. Mom hugged me so hard I couldn't finish. Sometimes adults make a thing sadder than it was when you started saying it.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 005 — Monday, November 2, 1998 — The Computer Argument


Dad let me watch him fix a C++ program tonight. He showed me a loop and I asked what happens if the condition never changes. He said the computer would keep going until somebody stopped it. I said that's a pretty stupid instruction. He said there is an entire profession devoted to making fewer stupid instructions.


He works at Microsoft and knows almost everything about computers but still can't find his glasses when they're on his head.


He says we'll write a little program together this winter. I'm going to make it argue back.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 006 — Friday, November 20, 1998 — Money


A girl at school said everyone who works at Microsoft is rich. I told her that's not true. Then she said my house is big and my dad drives a Volvo and we must be rich. I didn't know what to say because we are.


Dad explained stock options at dinner. It sounds like being paid with promises that might turn into money. He says being lucky is not the same thing as being better than someone.


I asked if that meant I could have a pony. He said no. Apparently there's a limit to what the stock market can do.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 007 — Friday, December 4, 1998 — Four Scrolls


At temple we talked about the Torahs that everyone carried when the congregation moved into the new building this spring. I remember the crowd and how carefully people held them. Mom cried a little, which she says is normal when something matters.


Our rabbi said we are supposed to ask questions. Good. Because I have about a thousand.


Maya thinks Hebrew letters look like little animals. I told her they look like letters. She says my imagination needs exercise. Maybe she's right. I drew a bird that looked like an aleph in the corner of my homework.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 008 — Wednesday, December 16, 1998 — Cars


Mom wouldn't let Dad rent a Mercedes when his Volvo went into the shop. The rental person must have thought she was insane. Mom said her parents would never buy a German car, and she won't either. Dad told me about Henry Ford saying hateful things about Jews.


I asked why we drive Volvos if they cost so much more than some other cars. Dad said choosing a car isn't always a math problem.


That seems suspiciously convenient when it's Dad saying it.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 009 — Sunday, December 27, 1998 — A Secret at Dinner


Mom and Dad told me something tonight. Mom is pregnant.


I stared at them so long Dad asked if I was all right. I am all right. I just didn't know you could be surprised and happy and scared all at once. Mom squeezed my hand. Dad looked happier than I've seen him in ages, but also sort of frightened.


I asked if the baby gets Rebecca's room. Mom said no, the baby will have its own room.


Good. That is the right answer.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 010 — Thursday, December 31, 1998 — Midnight


Mom went to bed early, so Dad and I stayed up until midnight with sparkling cider. He showed me pictures of the fireworks on television. Then he put on an old record and tried to teach me to dance in the kitchen.


I asked whether he and Mom still fight about the boat. He stopped dancing. He said they used to fight about it more than anything, and that sometimes people say things they can't take back, but they can learn how to live with each other afterward.


I don't know whether that's an answer. It is the most honest one he's given me.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 011 — Saturday, January 23, 1999 — Maya's Theory


Maya thinks the world is probably somebody's science project. I told her a science project would need a person outside the world to make it. She said maybe we are inside a much bigger world. I said then somebody would have to make that one too.


We argued all the way through lunch and then forgot the argument because she spilled orange juice on her shirt.


I like having a friend who can say something completely ridiculous and make me think about it for three days.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 012 — Saturday, February 13, 1999 — Paint


I painted the view from my window today. Mostly grey sky and the big cedar across the street. I tried to get the wet shine on the sidewalk right and made a purple puddle instead.


Dad said the purple puddle was his favorite part. Mom said I ought to try watercolors because I have no patience for waiting for anything to dry.


I don't think everything needs to be useful. Painting doesn't make me better at math. It just makes the afternoon go away in a lovely way.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 013 — Wednesday, March 17, 1999 — Names


Mom wants the baby's name to be Andrew if it's a boy. Dad likes Daniel. I like Andrew because I have already decided to call him Andy. When I told Dad that, he said the naming committee hadn't voted yet.


I think babies should get to rename themselves at twelve. What if you turn out nothing like the name your parents picked?


Mom says I was Elizabeth for eleven minutes before Dad started calling me Beth. She won't tell me what Rebecca would have called herself. Of course she can't. That's the point.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 014 — Friday, April 2, 1999 — Passover in Victoria


We're staying with Grandma Miriam and Grandpa Jakob for Passover. Grandpa keeps asking me questions about school as if he is checking whether the teachers deserve their salaries. Grandma makes everything seem effortless, even though she has cooked enough food for an army.


She showed me an old photograph of her sister Hanne in Denmark. Hanne lives in Israel now and has TEN children. Ten! I asked how she remembers which one she's angry with. Grandma laughed so hard she had to sit down.


I want to meet Hanne someday. She sounds like trouble.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 015 — Sunday, May 9, 1999 — Mother's Day


I made Mom breakfast and burned the toast. She ate it anyway, which proves mothers are either very loving or have defective taste buds.


Her stomach is getting round. She said the baby kicked during synagogue yesterday. I put my hand there but nothing happened. I think he's already stubborn.


Mom and Dad were laughing together while they washed dishes. I stood in the doorway watching them until Mom caught me and asked what I wanted.


Nothing, really. I just liked seeing them laugh.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 016 — Saturday, June 19, 1999 — Grandpa's Map


Grandpa Thomas brought a map of Alaska and showed me where he worked near Juneau before he married Grandma Nora. He met her at the mining office. I asked whether he loved her right away. He said he thought she was the cleverest woman he'd ever met and that was more dangerous than love at first sight.


Grandma Nora said he tells that story differently every time.


I wish I could go everywhere on the map. I don't want one of those lives where all the important things happen within ten miles of home.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 017 — Sunday, July 11, 1999 — The Hospital Bag


Mom put a bag by the front door today. I asked if she was moving out. Dad nearly choked on his coffee.


Baby Andy is due soon. Everyone says I'm going to be a wonderful big sister, which seems unfair because I haven't done anything yet.


I told Mom I know being a big sister isn't the same as being a twin. She said she knows. We didn't say anything for a while.


Then I asked if I could paint the baby's room with stars. She said yes, provided I don't paint the ceiling fan again. One mistake and they never forget.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 018 — Saturday, August 7, 1999 — The Boats


Seafair again. I can hear the engines even from far away. Mom hates this weekend. Dad tries not to say much about it.


People sometimes ask if I'm scared of boats. That's not the question. I remember the other boat coming, the hit, Rebecca sliding on the foredeck, and how I reached for her hand and nearly went over too. I remember her between the boats. I know what happened and who hit us. I was there.


We visited her grave today. I brought a little smooth stone. I told her she would have liked Maya, even though Maya talks too much.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 019 — Monday, August 16, 1999 — Andrew!


HE'S HERE.


Andrew David Peterson. Seven pounds something, a face like a squashed tomato, and hands so tiny I was afraid to touch them.


Dad cried when he showed me the baby. Actual tears. Mom was exhausted and grinning like she'd won a prize nobody else could see.


I held Andy while sitting in a chair with about twelve pillows around me. He opened one eye and sneezed. Mom says he already knows my voice.


I have so many things to tell him. I'm going to start with the cedar tree outside my window.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 020 — Friday, August 20, 1999 — New Rules


Apparently babies have no respect for schedules. Andy eats when he wants, sleeps when he wants, and makes noises like a sick duck.


Dad was walking around at three in the morning carrying him, talking about software bugs in a very serious voice. I couldn't stop laughing. Then Dad handed Andy to me and said, "Your turn, Senior Analyst."


I told Andy he could be anything he wants except a boy who leaves wet towels on the floor. Mom says it's too early to negotiate.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 021 — Saturday, September 11, 1999 — Beginning Again


It's Rosh Hashanah. At temple the rabbi talked about beginnings and about how a person can choose what to do differently this year.


I don't think you can just choose to be a new person. You still have all the old things inside you. But maybe that's not what beginning again means.


Mom held Andy through part of the service. Dad passed me the prayer book when I lost the place. For a minute I could see all four of us reflected in the window.


Four is a strange number for our family. I didn't say that aloud.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 022 — Monday, October 11, 1999 — Eleven


ELEVEN today. I have kept this diary for a WHOLE YEAR, except for all the days I didn't.


Grandma Miriam sent another book, Grandma Nora sent a scarf, and Maya gave me a pencil that says FUTURE GENIUS. Dad says I should keep it until we have evidence.


I went to see Rebecca with Mom. I said happy birthday out loud. She would have been eleven too. Mom asked whether I wanted to stay longer. I said no, I wanted to get home for cake.


Both things felt right. I don't see why they shouldn't.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 023 — Wednesday, November 24, 1999 — Probability


Dad showed me how to count all the possible outcomes when you throw two dice. I made a chart and discovered that seven comes up in more combinations than two. I wanted to test it about a million times but he said perhaps a hundred would do.


Later I thought about accidents. Dad said probability tells you how often something might happen, not what it feels like when it does.


I wrote that down because it seems important. Also because I beat him at our dice game three times in a row.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 024 — Friday, December 31, 1999 — The End of 1999


Everyone is talking about Y2K. Dad says people are panicking about clocks inside computers and that lots of programmers are spending New Year's Eve at work. I asked whether he has to go in. He said not unless something catches fire, which is not as reassuring as he thinks.


Maya called and said the whole world might shut down at midnight. I told her I would write an eyewitness report if it did.


Andy is asleep. Mom is making cocoa. Dad is checking his pager. The world is still here so far.


I hope next year is interesting. But not TOO interesting.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 025 — 2000-01-07 — Nothing Exploded


The computers survived New Year's Eve. Dad says that's partly because many people spent years fixing them, not because the problem was imaginary. Maya insists she personally saved civilization by staying awake until midnight.


I have started another page in the back of this book called Questions Nobody Answers Properly. Number one: if time is made of moments, how long is a moment? Number two: why does Andy laugh when you sneeze? The second one is harder.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 026 — 2000-01-22 — Andy's Teeth


Andy has a tooth coming in and has decided this is everyone's fault. I tried reading him a book about dinosaurs. He ate the corner.


Dad said I was exactly like that as a baby. I asked how he could possibly remember which twin did what. He said he doesn't always. I was annoyed, then relieved. I don't remember everything either.


Maya says I'm getting sentimental. I told her she is getting taller without permission.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 027 — 2000-02-14 — Valentine's Day Is Ridiculous


Someone left a paper heart on my desk. It had no name. I thought it was from Owen because he borrowed my colored pencils yesterday, but he said hearts are stupid.


I told Maya I didn't care who left it. We spent forty minutes trying to work out who did.


Dad came home with flowers for Mom. She said he didn't have to. He said that wasn't the point. I am increasingly convinced grown-ups say things that mean the opposite of their words.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 028 — 2000-03-05 — The Family Photograph


Mom finally put a new family photograph on the mantel. Dad, Mom, me and Andy in his ridiculous blue sweater. The old picture of the four of us with Rebecca is still beside it.


I thought Mom was going to move the old one. She didn't. She just dusted both frames.


I liked that more than if she had made a speech about it. I'm learning that sometimes things are easier when nobody explains them.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 029 — 2000-04-21 — A Question at the Seder


At Passover in Victoria I asked Grandpa Jakob why his family chose Canada while Great-Aunt Hanne went to Israel. He said when the war was over, nobody knew where life would be safe or what being safe even meant. People made decisions with what they knew then.


Hanne has ten children, so Grandma says the family telephone bill between Victoria and Israel could finance a small country.


I asked whether Grandpa ever wishes he'd gone there too. He looked at Grandma and said, "Not when I look at what I have here."


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 030 — 2000-05-12 — The Volcano Painting


I painted a mountain with a red volcano coming out of the top. Maya said it looked like Mount Rainier having a terrible day. I think that's an excellent description.


Our teacher wanted to put it in the hallway, but I said no because I'd drawn little people running away and one of them had six fingers.


Why do paintings have to look like the real thing? I can see the real thing any time. What I can't see is a red volcano above a purple lake with six-fingered people fleeing it.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 031 — 2000-06-30 — No More School


Summer! I'm going to read five books, learn to make a computer game, improve my swimming, and stay up late every night.


Dad says I should budget my time. Mom says I'm a child, not a project manager. They argued over which of them is responsible for my tendency to write lists.


Andy has learned to clap. He clapped when I fell off the couch. Our house contains absolutely no respect for genius.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 032 — 2000-08-06 — The Day We Don't Go


It's Seafair again. Dad offered to take me somewhere fun today, anywhere I wanted except the lake. We went to a bookstore and then got noodles. I chose three books and he bought four because he has no self-control either.


Mom went to Rebecca's grave in the morning. I went with her. We left stones and stood there until she said she was ready.


Dad drove us home. Nobody argued. Later he made pancakes for dinner. I like pancakes for dinner. They feel like a small rebellion.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 033 — 2000-09-03 — New Shoes


Got new school shoes. They're comfortable but look like something a nurse would wear. Mom says practical shoes are a blessing. Mom is not eleven.


Maya cut her hair so short that half the girls in our class are calling her a boy. She doesn't care, or says she doesn't. I told her she looks like a movie star who has just escaped from prison. That made her laugh.


Tomorrow I am wearing the impractical shoes from last year until my feet fall off.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 034 — 2000-10-11 — Twelve


Twelve. I had wanted to feel different this morning, but the bathroom mirror showed exactly the same face as yesterday.


Maya gave me earrings shaped like tiny planets. Dad pretended to be upset because they were arranged in the wrong order from the sun.


I had a dream about Rebecca last night. We were playing cards and she was annoyed that I kept changing the rules. I woke up laughing. I told Mom, and she laughed too. That may be the nicest part of today.


Also: chocolate cake. Again. We are people of tradition.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 035 — 2000-11-19 — Dad's Religion


I asked Dad if becoming Jewish meant he stopped believing what he believed when he was Methodist. He said some things changed and some didn't. I asked whether he'd have converted if he hadn't met Mom. He said probably not.


"Then how do you know you chose it for yourself?" I asked.


He thought about that for a long time. Then he said, "Sometimes another person opens a door, and you still have to decide whether to walk through."


I liked the answer but I still think I won.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 036 — 2000-12-28 — An Empty Afternoon


Nothing happened today.


I finished a book, ruined a watercolor by adding too much yellow, ate three cookies, and made Andy laugh by putting a sock on my hand and calling it Professor Foot.


I don't know why I'm writing this. Maybe diaries are supposed to be about days when things happen, but that's silly. Most days aren't like that. I don't want to forget all the ordinary ones.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 037 — 2001-01-15 — The Bat Mitzvah Question


The rabbi asked what I want people to remember about my bat mitzvah later this year. I said I want to read Hebrew without making a fool of myself. She said that's a reasonable goal but perhaps not the whole point.


Mom wants a big family celebration. Dad says I should decide what kind of party I want.


I want my grandmothers there. I want Maya there. I want a cake that tastes good, not one that's beautiful and dry. Surely thirteen years of existence have earned me that.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 038 — 2001-02-28 — Earthquake!


The floor moved today. Really moved! At first I thought somebody was shaking my chair, then all the chairs were shaking. Everybody went quiet in a way I've never heard at school.


Mom called as soon as the phones worked properly. Dad was at Microsoft and said their building swayed. Nobody in our family was hurt.


I keep testing the floor with my feet. I know that's not scientific. I can't help it.


Maya says the Earth was reminding us who is in charge. I said the Earth doesn't have intentions. She said that's exactly what the Earth wants me to think.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 039 — 2001-03-18 — Grandma Nora's Hair


Grandma Nora let me brush her hair. She's gone greyer, but underneath I can see the same brown-black as mine. She told me a few stories about her mother in Juneau and said some family stories are hers to tell and some belonged to people who aren't here to correct them.


I asked whether I should say I'm Native too. She said I should tell the truth about my family without borrowing anybody else's life.


Then she made me brush out a knot I'd created. Wisdom is apparently very inconvenient.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 040 — 2001-04-08 — First Crush, Maybe


There is a boy named Lucas who can make me forget what I was about to say. This is not an improvement.


He asked me for help with fractions. I explained them twice and then forgot the answer to my own example. He said I was funny. I was trying to be brilliant.


Maya says I have a crush. I told her a crush implies evidence. She said my face was the evidence.


I would like to request a different face.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 041 — 2001-05-26 — The Rabbi and the Question


At temple I asked why God would need people to say prayers if God already knows what they think. Our rabbi said prayer isn't supposed to inform God; it can change the person praying.


I said I still don't understand why that would require Hebrew.


She smiled and said that's a good question for next week.


I like her. She never treats questions like bad manners. Mom says I should remember to let other people talk sometimes. I feel this criticism is only partly fair.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 042 — 2001-06-16 — A Lake Without Boats


Went to a park near the water with Maya. We sat on the grass eating chips and talking about whether we'd rather be famous or invisible. I picked invisible. She said I couldn't bear not telling everyone what I had discovered.


I was looking at the lake and remembered the deck of the Sea Ray, the sun, the impact, Becca going over. I didn't tell Maya right then. We were talking about other things. I wasn't trying to hide anything.


On the way home I told her I'd changed my mind. I'd rather be famous for writing a book. She said she'd rather have a horse.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 043 — 2001-08-19 — The Book Grandma Didn't Finish


Grandma Miriam gave me a Danish children's book she'd saved. She tried reading it aloud but kept stopping to explain words and tell me stories about her childhood. After an hour we'd read two pages.


I asked whether she remembered Denmark before the war. She said she remembered a staircase, a neighbor's yellow cat, and the smell of bread, and wasn't certain which memories were hers and which came from photographs.


That's strange. History books make everything look arranged in the correct order. Grandma's life doesn't fit in neat chapters.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 044 — 2001-09-11 — Today


Something terrible happened in New York and Washington today. The teachers were quiet and a television was on in another room. I saw pictures of the buildings burning. I kept thinking the pictures couldn't be real, even after they showed them again.


Dad came home early. We ate dinner together without the television. Mom called Grandma in Victoria and then some of the family in Israel.


I don't have an opinion about what it all means. I just wish the people on the news could go home.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 045 — 2001-09-19 — Too Many Opinions


Everyone has started explaining what happened last week. Adults on television sound certain about things they didn't seem to know yesterday.


At temple people were worried and angry and trying to help. I asked Dad how you can know who is telling the truth when everybody talks with the same confident voice. He said to look for evidence and to be suspicious of people who never admit what they don't know.


I am suspicious of him now because he said that very confidently.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 046 — 2001-10-11 — Thirteen


Thirteen today. My birthday is on a Thursday, and my bat mitzvah is Saturday, so the whole week feels like one enormous school assignment.


Mom and I visited Rebecca. I told her I'm going to read from the Torah and I'm afraid I'll stumble over the same word twice. Mom said Rebecca would have been teasing me. I said she would probably have been just as nervous, and we'd have practiced together until we were both sick of it.


I am excited too. It's possible to be both. Apparently thirteen is already complicated.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 047 — 2001-10-13 — Bat Mitzvah


I DID IT.


I read my portion, forgot to breathe once, and found my place again. Grandma Nora cried, Grandma Miriam cried, Mom cried, and Dad tried to pretend he wasn't crying. Maya grinned at me from the second row like an idiot.


Afterward people kept calling me a young woman, which seems premature since I still can't find my other shoe.


Dad danced with Mom at the party. Andy fell asleep on Grandpa Jakob's lap.


I thought I would feel different afterward. Mostly I feel hungry and happy and very, very tired.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 048 — 2001-11-04 — Three Versions of Me


Apparently there's the Beth my teachers know, the Beth my parents know, and the Beth who talks to Maya about absolutely everything.


I don't think any of them is fake. They're just not the whole thing.


I wonder if that's what adults mean when they say someone is "finding herself." You don't find one person. You keep discovering extra rooms.


That sounded intelligent when I wrote it. I may cross it out tomorrow.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 049 — 2001-12-22 — A Letter from Israel


A cousin in Israel sent photographs of Great-Aunt Hanne at a family dinner. There are so many people around the table that I can't work out who belongs to whom.


Mom says Hanne served as an officer in the army long ago. I asked whether she really did secret work afterward. Mom said some family stories are stories and some are things people don't discuss.


That is the least satisfying answer anyone could have given me.


I want to go to Israel. I also want to go to Denmark and Alaska. Maybe everywhere.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 050 — 2002-01-08 — Not a Great Day


Maya and I had a stupid fight. She said I always correct people and sometimes it feels like I want them to feel stupid. I said I only correct things that are wrong, which was precisely the wrong thing to say.


I thought about it during dinner and got mad at her again. Then I thought about it more and got mad at myself.


I called her. I said I was sorry for making her feel that way. She said she was sorry for calling me a walking encyclopedia with hair.


We are friends again. I still think encyclopedias are wonderful.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 051 — 2002-02-17 — The History of a Teacup


We were at Grandma Miriam's in Victoria. I picked up a chipped blue teacup and she told me it belonged to her mother in Denmark. It had been packed, shipped, unpacked, and moved into at least five different kitchens.


I said that's a very long history for one ugly cup.


Grandma said history is mostly ordinary objects surviving people who thought they were ordinary too.


I looked at the cup differently after that. Then she made tea in it, proving that historical artifacts can still be useful.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 052 — 2002-03-31 — New Paintbrushes


I bought two good brushes with my birthday money. Dad says spending more doesn't automatically make something better. I told him nobody spends as much on computer parts as he does.


He said that's different. Of course it is.


I'm working on a painting of our kitchen at night, with just the lamp over the table. Everything looks green and gold and quiet. I keep leaving Andy out because he never stays still long enough to paint. Maybe I'll put his toy dinosaur on the floor instead.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 053 — 2002-05-05 — Lucas at the Dance


Lucas asked me to dance at the school party. I stepped on his foot. Not lightly.


He said he liked talking to me because I never agreed with anything without asking why. I couldn't tell whether that was a compliment, but he looked very pleased with himself.


We danced again. I didn't step on him that time.


When I told Maya, she said I was smiling like a lunatic. I reminded her that she'd once cried over a boy who couldn't spell her name. She said this was not relevant evidence.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 054 — 2002-06-21 — End of Eighth Grade


Eighth grade is over and I have discovered that being good at tests doesn't make the last week any less boring.


Mom wants us to visit Victoria in July. Dad wants a mountain trip. Andrew wants a fire truck. I want all three, though preferably not simultaneously.


Lucas wrote his phone number in my yearbook even though I already have it. Maya says boys are a mystery. I think boys are fairly simple, except when I am talking to one I actually like.


Then all the words in my head get in each other's way.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 055 — 2002-07-17 — The Mountains


We went hiking with Dad. He carried Andy when the trail got steep and claimed he was building endurance. I said he was building a hernia.


We stopped beside a cold stream. I drew the bend in the water while Dad tried to explain how moving water chooses its path. I told him it doesn't choose, it just moves. He said that's what makes the question interesting.


When we got home Mom kissed him and said he smelled like an exhausted bear. He said she married him voluntarily. Apparently that argument can end in kissing.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 056 — 2002-08-09 — The Date I Dreaded


I don't know why people say you "get over" losing someone. You don't climb over a person and leave them behind.


It's Seafair. Mom visited Rebecca's grave early and I went later with Dad. He didn't talk about the collision. Neither did I. I know what I saw then. I don't need to explain it every year to prove I remember her.


I told Dad about Lucas instead. He asked whether Lucas was nice to me. I said yes. Dad looked relieved, which was sweet and slightly embarrassing.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 057 — 2002-09-04 — Junior High, Again


Ninth grade began. Last year at junior high, they say. Next year we'll be real high school students, which sounds both exciting and suspicious.


There are people in my classes I've known for years and still know practically nothing about. There are also people who can remember every embarrassing thing I have ever done.


Maya is in two of my classes and Lucas only one. I spent the entire morning pretending that didn't matter. It mattered.


I need a new notebook for algebra. Not for this diary. This diary is nobody's business.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 058 — 2002-09-28 — Truth and Apologies


The rabbi spoke about the coming days of reflection, and afterward I asked whether saying sorry counts if you mostly want the other person to stop being angry.


She said it's better to be honest about your motives than to pretend they're pure.


I thought about the time I apologized to Maya just because I missed having somebody to tell things to. I was sorry, but I was also lonely. Maybe both can be true.


Dad says grown-up decisions are often like that. He looked tired when he said it.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 059 — 2002-10-11 — Fourteen


Fourteen! Grandpa Jakob says fourteen is twice seven and seven is a lucky number in many traditions, therefore I'm doubly lucky. I told him that's not how probability works. He said I sound just like my father and ordered more cake.


Andrew sang Happy Birthday at the top of his lungs, mostly on one note. Maya gave me a small silver charm shaped like a book.


Rebecca would be fourteen. I wondered today whether she'd have liked Lucas. I think she would have thought he was sweet and then stolen him just to irritate me. That's not sadness. That's knowing your sister.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 060 — 2002-11-03 — The Experiment


Dad and I wrote a little program to shuffle a deck of cards. I told him his algorithm wasn't random enough. He told me to prove it. We spent the afternoon testing outcomes while Mom shouted from the hallway that normal people occasionally went outside.


I love it when Dad treats me like someone worth arguing with.


Later I found a note from Lucas asking whether I want to go to a movie next weekend. I stared at it longer than we spent debugging the code. Humans are embarrassingly inefficient.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 061 — 2002-12-27 — Three Days of Snow


Snow made everything quiet, then slushy. I wanted the first part to last longer.


At dinner Grandpa Thomas told a mining story that changed twice while he was telling it. Grandma Nora interrupted him both times. I asked how anyone is supposed to know what really happened. She said to listen to everyone who was there, then remember they each saw a different piece.


I told her I might study history someday. Dad looked pleased. Mom looked even more pleased.


Andy asked if historians get to dig up dinosaurs. I said no. He said he won't be one then.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 062 — 2003-01-03 — Bad Resolutions


Maya and I made a list of things to do this year. Hers included learning guitar, mine included finishing twelve books and not interrupting people.


By lunchtime I had interrupted her four times, and she said she would be surprised if I lasted until February.


I don't understand why people start being better only on January first. On the other hand, I did like writing the list on fresh paper. Maybe the paper helps.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 063 — 2003-01-27 — The Hair Disaster


I tried making my hair straight with a borrowed flat iron. It took forever, smelled funny, and made me look like someone had placed a very serious curtain around my face.


Mom said she loved my natural waves. Of course she did. She didn't spend an hour doing this.


Maya came over and said I looked like Dad's computer monitor when the screen saver was off. I have no idea what that means, but I laughed so hard I had to wash my hair again.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 064 — 2003-02-15 — Lucas's Sweater


Lucas gave me a little box of chocolates yesterday. I gave him a handmade bookmark. I spent twenty minutes imagining this meant something tremendous.


Today he wore the ugliest striped sweater I've ever seen and said his grandmother knitted it. Suddenly I liked the sweater.


I wonder whether liking somebody means objects become better when they belong to that person. It would explain a lot of truly horrible romantic poetry.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 065 — 2003-03-13 — Science Fair


Miles Turner informed me that my statistics demonstration was "basically just counting." I told him all of mathematics is counting if you're determined to be stupid about it.


He grinned, which made me angrier. Then he helped me fix the graph I'd accidentally printed backwards. He was right about one part of my sample size.


I hate when a person I'm arguing with is useful. Perhaps I should add that to my resolutions.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 066 — 2003-04-20 — The Quiet House


Dad was away at a Microsoft conference and Mom had a meeting, so I watched Andy for two hours. He wanted me to build a castle, then destroyed it every time I finished a wall.


I told him architects don't usually encourage demolition. He told me dragons do.


After he went to bed I sat on the floor beside the blocks. The house felt huge. It must have seemed even bigger to Mom after Rebecca died.


Then Mom came home with ice cream and I stopped feeling philosophical.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 067 — 2003-05-11 — Our Mothers


Maya complained that her mom asks too many questions. I said at least her mom asks; mine can sometimes finish my answer before I begin.


Then I felt bad. Mom listened to me complain about school for forty minutes and never once mentioned she was tired. She had been working on a charity auction all afternoon.


I told her afterward that I loved her. She said, "What have you done?"


I said, "Nothing yet." She laughed. I really must stop giving her reasons to be suspicious.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 068 — 2003-06-18 — Goodbye, Junior High


We signed yearbooks and pretended we'd never see one another again, though most of us are going to the same high school.


Lucas kissed me on the cheek beside the gym. It lasted about half a second. I thought about it for the entire bus ride home.


Maya says I should stop trying to explain everything. She says the experience is allowed to happen without a theory.


I am considering the possibility she is right. Please don't tell her.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 069 — 2003-07-06 — Walla Walla


We drove through eastern Washington to visit family friends and stopped in Walla Walla. It looked nothing like Redmond. The sky seemed enormous and dry, and everybody talked about wheat, wine, or how hot it was.


We walked past a college with lovely old buildings and trees. Whitman. I liked the name and the quiet streets around it.


Dad asked whether I could imagine living in a place like this. I said no, then kept thinking about it all evening. It would be strange to be somewhere nobody knew my family.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 070 — 2003-08-03 — Seafair Without Us


The boats were on television today. Andy wanted to watch them. Mom changed the channel. Dad put down the newspaper.


I told Andy about the little boats I'd made out of paper when I was small. That distracted him for approximately four minutes.


Later Dad asked whether I minded talking about boats. I said no. I mind when everybody acts as though one word might break the furniture. He said he understood. I'm not certain he does, but I'm glad he asked.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 071 — 2003-08-26 — New Building, New Me?


We toured Redmond High before school begins. The building is new and smells like paint and floor wax. The lockers seemed enormous until I tried to open mine.


Mom asked if I was excited. I told her a building doesn't change your personality. She said sometimes a new place makes people brave enough to show a different part of it.


I think that is probably true, although I don't intend to say so in front of her.


High school next week. I have bought three notebooks and an unreasonable amount of lip gloss.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 072 — 2003-09-03 — High School


First day at Redmond High. I got lost between classes and found the science rooms by accident, which was fine until I realized the bell had rung.


My history teacher, Ms. Chen, asked why we study people who are already dead. I said because their decisions are still affecting us. She wrote it on the board without saying whether it was right.


I like her.


Lucas looks older than he did in June. Unfortunately he knows it.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 073 — 2003-09-25 — The Argument About Money


A boy in class said people who live in our neighborhood don't know what real problems are. I opened my mouth to argue and stopped. There were about six different things I could have said, some true and some nasty.


At dinner I told Dad. He said our money solves many problems and doesn't solve others. He also said I don't need to apologize for having a comfortable life, but shouldn't pretend it hasn't made things easier.


I hate answers where nobody gets to win.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 074 — 2003-10-11 — Fifteen


Fifteen. I had a birthday dinner with Maya, Lucas, and three friends from school. Dad grilled salmon badly. Mom rescued the vegetables. Andy made a paper crown and insisted I wear it during dessert.


Mom and I took flowers to Rebecca first. I told her about Lucas and admitted that I don't think she would have liked his hair. I could almost hear her laughing.


I don't know what sixteen will be like. Fifteen seems ridiculous enough already.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 075 — 2003-10-31 — A Terrible Party


Went to a Halloween party dressed as a mathematician. Nobody could tell I was in costume. Maya found this hysterical.


Lucas spent most of the evening with some boys from the soccer team. I stood with the girls pretending I was having the time of my life. I was not.


On the ride home I told Maya I thought Lucas was ignoring me. She asked whether I'd tried talking to him. I said I shouldn't have to.


She said, "Beth, you can prove things on paper, but you can't expect boys to read your mind."


I dislike her wisdom.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 076 — 2003-11-16 — A Boyfriend, Apparently


Lucas called to apologize for the Halloween party. Then he said he thought we were going out, and I said I thought so too, and we both went silent.


So, apparently, I have a boyfriend.


I told Mom. She asked whether he was kind. Not whether he was Jewish, rich, intelligent, or from a good family. Just kind.


I said yes, mostly. She said "mostly" is a word worth paying attention to. Sometimes she says one sentence and somehow leaves me with twelve problems.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 077 — 2003-12-07 — Eight Candles


Lighting candles at home tonight felt especially good. Andy insisted on putting the shamash in the wrong place because he said it was the boss candle and deserved its own spot.


Dad told the Hanukkah story. Mom corrected two historical details. I corrected a third. Andy asked whether the ancient Greeks had dinosaurs.


This family is going to take eight nights to finish one conversation.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 078 — 2004-01-19 — What I Want


Mrs. Chen asked us to write about the person we want to become. I filled a page with words like educated, independent, accomplished, useful.


Then I crossed out accomplished because I didn't know accomplished at what.


I don't want to spend my life doing something only because I am good at it. I like math, but I also love history. I like painting even when I'm bad at it. I like making people laugh.


How do adults choose just one thing? Maybe they don't. Maybe that is the secret.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 079 — 2004-02-08 — The Non-Fight


Lucas was irritated because I corrected his story in front of his friends. I said the date mattered. He said the date wasn't the point.


We walked around Redmond Town Center without talking. Finally I asked whether he wanted me to pretend to believe things I knew weren't true. He said no, he wanted me to stop performing an oral examination whenever he told a story.


I didn't apologize immediately. I wish I had. Two days later I did. It was much harder by then.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 080 — 2004-03-06 — Old Fire House


Maya dragged me to a show at the Old Fire House Teen Center. The band was loud and not particularly good, but they played as if the whole world might end if they stopped.


One guitarist broke a string and kept going. People cheered.


I have never understood music like this before. It didn't need to be perfect to be exciting. We went home with ringing ears and the names of three bands written on our wrists.


I'm making a painting of the guitarist. I hope he never sees it.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 081 — 2004-03-29 — Dad's Promotion That Wasn't


Dad's team finished something important at Microsoft and Mom opened a bottle of sparkling wine to celebrate. I asked if he was getting promoted. He said no, just getting the satisfaction of fixing a difficult problem.


Then I asked what his job title actually meant. Senior analyst, he said, as if that settled everything.


He showed me an ugly little piece of C++ code and explained why it was elegant. I told him that if it were elegant, it should look prettier. He said I had a lot to learn about elegance.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 082 — 2004-04-14 — The Cemetery


Stopped at Rebecca's grave with Mom after an appointment in town. It was damp and the grass needed cutting. Somebody had left a small stone beside ours. Mom said maybe Grandma Miriam had visited.


I wondered whether Rebecca would have wanted to be a scientist or an artist or a complete nuisance. There isn't a correct answer.


Mom asked whether we should go. I said in a minute. We stayed longer than a minute, then went for sandwiches. Ordinary life doesn't wait politely outside a cemetery.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 083 — 2004-05-22 — Nobody Is Normal


Maya confessed she's scared she'll disappoint her parents if she doesn't get into a good college. I told her she could become a famous guitarist and disappoint them spectacularly.


She laughed and then cried a little, which made me stop joking.


I think I've been unfair to her. I assumed because she acts fearless she must feel fearless. I probably do the opposite: I act certain when I'm uncertain.


She told me not to put that in my diary. I'm putting it in my diary. Sorry, Maya.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 084 — 2004-06-15 — The Last Day of Tenth


Exams are over. I got the highest score in math and a B+ on a history paper because Mrs. Chen said my argument was excellent but I hadn't cited enough sources.


I complained to Dad, who asked whether she was right. I said yes but that wasn't the point.


Lucas wants to go to a concert next month. Maya wants us to drive out to the coast. Mom wants me to help with Andy's birthday plans. I want three weeks when nobody asks me to decide anything.


Naturally everybody asked me where we should eat dinner.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 085 — 2004-07-04 — Independence Day


We spent the afternoon with neighbors. I helped a little girl paint stars on paper cups while the adults debated property taxes and schools.


One man said children who grow up with money never learn independence. I wanted to tell him independence isn't a bank balance, but Mom shook her head slightly.


Afterward she said I was welcome to disagree with him, but she didn't want me to fight her battles for her. I hadn't realized it was her battle.


My mother is much more mysterious than she pretends to be.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 086 — 2004-07-27 — The Trip We Didn't Take


Lucas and I were going to a movie, but he called and said he needed to help his father. I was irritated and decided not to say so because I didn't want to sound needy.


Then I spent the evening making myself miserable, which is apparently preferable to telling the truth.


He called again after dinner and we talked for an hour. His dad had hurt his back. I felt awful about my private little drama.


I need to remember that not every disappointment is a message about me.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 087 — 2004-08-07 — Ten Years


Ten years since the accident. I remember Rebecca's face clearly, and her hand leaving mine. I also remember the noise of the impact and knowing another boat hit us. I don't need anyone to tell me whose fault that collision was.


Mom and Dad went to the cemetery together. Dad stood beside her with an arm around her shoulders. Sometimes I'm astonished that they found a way back to each other.


Later we had dinner at home and Andy told a joke so dreadful that we all laughed until we couldn't breathe. We needed that.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 088 — 2004-08-29 — A Room Full of Books


We were in Victoria. Grandpa Jakob showed me the records from one of his early real estate deals. He and Grandma bought a building that needed repairs, fixed it, rented the apartments, and used what they'd earned to buy another.


"That's how people become wealthy?" I asked.


"Sometimes," he said. "Other times they do exactly the same thing and lose everything."


I liked his answer. He showed me the old bills and photographs. I think I love the documents more than the buildings.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 089 — 2004-09-09 — Eleventh Grade


The first week of junior year is over. People keep talking about college as though it's a train we all have to catch or we'll be stranded forever.


Miles Turner is in my advanced math class. He has become taller and no less irritating. He says I think like a historian when I should think like a mathematician.


I told him he thinks like a calculator that learned sarcasm. He laughed.


It bothers me that I look forward to our arguments.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 090 — 2004-09-26 — A Letter to Hanne


I wrote Great-Aunt Hanne a letter. Mom helped with a few Hebrew phrases and corrected my spelling. I asked Hanne what it was like being an army officer and whether she really had ten children without ever losing her mind.


Mom made me remove the last question. I put it back.


I also asked whether she thinks living in Israel feels different from living in a place where you're one Jewish family among lots of different kinds of people.


I hope she answers the questions I actually asked and not the ones Mom wishes I'd asked.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 091 — 2004-10-11 — Sixteen


Sixteen today, and I can finally say the word without sounding as if I'm borrowing somebody else's age.


Dad gave me a set of drawing pencils and promised more driving practice. Mom gave me a silver necklace that belonged to Grandma Miriam. Maya gave me a mix CD with songs she claims will improve my taste.


Lucas kissed me after the birthday dinner. It was a good kiss. I will not be making graphs about it, despite what Miles says.


I went to bed happy, then thought about Rebecca turning sixteen too. I wished her a happy birthday in the dark.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 092 — 2004-10-29 — Driving Lessons


Dad took me out to practice in the Volvo. He says the trick is to look far down the road instead of directly in front of the car. I asked whether that was also a philosophy of life. He said only when his daughter is trying to be clever.


We managed twenty minutes without either of us shouting. A miracle.


Mom refuses to buy me a German car when I finally get my license. I said I could live with a Toyota. Dad said that's probably the most expensive sentence I've ever spoken.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 093 — 2004-11-12 — The Reply


A letter came from Hanne! Her handwriting is like barbed wire.


She answered the question about her children first: "They lost my mind for me, one piece at a time, and then brought it back at Shabbat dinners."


She said Israel is neither a miracle that solves every problem nor a place she would trade for anywhere else. She did not answer my army question properly. She wrote, "Some things are better asked face to face."


I have put the letter inside the back cover of this diary. I'm going to Israel someday, and I'm going to ask her everything.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 094 — 2004-12-03 — A Fight in the Library


Lucas said I always have to be the cleverest person in the room. I said he only notices when I'm right. He said that was exactly what he meant.


We fought in whispers between the history shelves. It was ridiculous. Then I said something about his grades that I knew would hurt him, and it did.


I came home furious at him and ashamed of myself. I don't get to excuse being cruel just because somebody irritated me first.


I called to apologize. He hasn't called back. I don't blame him.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 095 — 2004-12-12 — Two Apologies


Lucas finally called. He said he was sorry for trying to make me feel small because he felt insecure. I said I was sorry for choosing the one thing I knew he was worried about and using it against him.


Neither apology made the fight vanish immediately. We talked about other things, and then stopped talking, and then talked again.


I think we are still together. I'm not sure what that means at sixteen, except that I'd like to try.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 096 — 2004-12-25 — Christmas at Someone Else's House


Maya's family invited me for Christmas dinner. There were so many decorations I wondered whether the house had been attacked by glitter.


Her grandmother asked whether being Jewish meant I'd never had a Christmas present. I said my family gives presents all the time, we just don't need a tree to justify it.


Maya kicked me under the table. Hard.


It was lovely, though. Her father played old songs on the piano and everybody sang badly. I went home smelling of cinnamon and wished our families ate together more often.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 097 — 2004-12-31 — A List I Won't Keep


My resolutions for 2005:
Read more. Paint more. Stop correcting people in front of their friends. Learn to drive without terrifying Dad. Figure out college. Ask better questions. Be nicer to Lucas. Visit Grandma more.


I want to travel and fall in love and know things nobody has ever explained to me properly. I also want to sleep until noon tomorrow.


I'm not certain a person can become who she wants to be using a list. But I like the list anyway.


Happy New Year, diary. We're still here.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 098 — 2005-01-08 — An Unexpected Ending


Lucas and I talked for a long time after school. He wants to spend less time trying to make us into a perfect couple and more time simply being friends. I knew what he meant before he said it.


I cried when I got home. Not because he was awful. Because he wasn't.


Maya brought over ice cream and didn't say one intelligent thing. I was so grateful. She just sat with me and told stories about people at school until I laughed.


I still have the silly bookmark I made him. I can't decide whether to ask for it back.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 099 — 2005-01-18 — After Lucas


It's strange how a person can be part of your ordinary day and then suddenly not be. I still look toward the spot where Lucas used to wait after class.


I am not dying of heartbreak. I had dinner, finished my homework, and laughed at something Miles said. But I miss him.


Dad asked if I wanted to talk. I said not yet. He brought me tea and left it by the door. That was better than a speech.


────────────────────────────────────


ENTRY 100 — 2005-02-06 — The Applications Before the Applications


Mom brought home brochures for colleges. UW, Whitman, some places on the East Coast. Dad says I should visit campuses rather than choose by the photographs.


I keep coming back to Whitman and remembering the huge sky over Walla Walla. I don't know why it keeps tugging at me.


Aunt Hanne hasn't written again. Grandma says she's busy keeping half of Israel in order. I told her I'd like a grandmother like that.


Grandma said, "You have several already." She's right.


────────────────────────────────────
